body.text: Few places or corridors tell a richer story of geography and human movement than Battle of Manila (1574). Stepping into its history reveals how trade, terrain, and culture shaped the modern map.

The Battle of Manila (1574) (Spanish: Batalla de Manila de 1574, Filipino: Labanan sa Maynila ng 1574) was fought on 29 November 1574 between Chinese and Japanese pirates led by Limahong and Spanish colonial forces with their native allies. It took place near Manila, mainly in what is now Parañaque, in the Philippines.
It marked the first time the Spanish directly clashed with the Japanese, who had occasionally tried to colonize the Philippines and claim sovereignty over it.

Limahong's fleet landed at Parañaque and from there began to assault the fortifications of Intramuros. Initially, the inhabitants were disorganized and Limahong's forces gained the advantage. The Chinese also killed the Spanish maestre de campo, Martín de Goiti. This delayed their assault on Manila, since Goiti's house blocked their march.

Limahong's forces laid siege to Manila but were halted by the fortifications and by defenders under Governor Guido de Lavezaris, who were later reinforced by fifty Spanish arquebusiers led by Juan de Salcedo.

After his defeat at Manila, Limahong abandoned his plans to take the city and instead settled in Pangasinan. The following year, a Spanish fleet led by Salcedo pursued Limahong, who escaped with part of his force.

This led the Viceroy of Fukien to travel to the Philippines to secure Limahong's return to China, but the mission ultimately established diplomatic relations between China and the Spanish Philippines.
Background

The first Spanish expedition arrived in the region in 1565, but the city was not founded until 1571. Once established, Manila became a center of commerce for multiple nations from South Asia as well as China and Japan, which traded porcelain, silk, and wood.
Manila's fame as a prosperous city spread quickly around southern Asia, attracting the interest of pirates and marauders.

In 1574, Chinese warlord Limahong had just been expelled from China by the imperial fleet in a battle in Guangdong. He was looking to move his headquarters to the Philippine islands, where he could obtain greater gains with less difficulty.

After capturing a Chinese trading ship that carried Spanish sailors, he learned that Manila had a garrison of only about 200 Spanish soldiers, and judged that it would be easy to capture the city in a surprise attack.

In November, guided by Spanish prisoners, Limahong arrived in Luzón with a fleet to expel the Spaniards and take the city. He left only a small part of his force on the island of Batán, where he had taken refuge from the Chinese imperial fleet.
Opposing forces

According to Spanish records, both sides were evenly matched in weapons and equipment. The key differences were the superior experience and training of the Spanish soldiers, their defensive positions, the timely arrival of reinforcements, and other tactical considerations. Both armies employed arquebuses and artillery pieces, as well as swords, daggers, and polearms.
Spanish

The garrison of Manila was composed of 200 Spanish soldiers. Half were Iberian, while the other half were of Mesoamerican origin, including both mestizos and indios amigos. The city was unprepared after a long period of peace, and the old fort built by Miguel López de Legazpi was badly maintained.
Sino-Japanese

Limahong's fleet was composed of 60 to 72 junks, and comprised 2,000 soldiers, 2,000 sailors, and 1,500 colonists, including entire families, women captured for ransom in China and Japan, farmers, carpenters, artisans, doctors, and all the goods necessary to establish a settlement.
A fleet of this size had probably been assembled from multiple ports around the sea, where its members lurked disguised as peaceful merchantmen while waiting for orders to rendezvous.

Although Limahong was Chinese, his pirate armada was a mix of Chinese and Japanese, along with other Asian ethnicities. According to historian Kenji Igawa, Chinese records show he acted in alliance with factions of wokou.

Limahong's lieutenant was a Japanese man called Sioco in Spanish sources, a name that Yosaburō Takekoshi identified as a corruption of the Japanese name Shogo. Spanish sources also describe the invaders as wielding catanes, a corruption of the Japanese word katana, as well as more traditional Chinese weapons, scimitars, sabers, and daggers.
It is also apparent that he had a Portuguese translator in his fleet.
Spanish chronicles describe in detail the arms and armor of Shogo's contingent, which historian Stephen Turnbull identifies as period Japanese military gear.

The pirates are described as carrying battle standards fastened to their bearers' shoulders like sashimono, cutlasses and daggers tucked into their belts in a manner evoking the daishō, straight spears like the yari, and long-bladed polearms (described as "enough by themselves to undo the thickest hauberks"), probably referring to the naginata.
The pirates also used many gunpowder hand grenades and incendiary devices, which Turnbull identifies as the Japanese grenade called horokubiya.
Battle

Limahong's armada was spotted by Spanish posts at Villa Fernandina in northern Luzón, commanded by Juan de Salcedo and Francisco de Saavedra. Alarmed by the size of the fleet, Salcedo believed it was a Portuguese fleet coming to attack Manila, so he gathered fifty arquebusiers in seven oared vessels to reinforce the city.

He also recruited 200 Ilocano warriors upon reaching Bauang. Meanwhile, he sent three messengers by sea to warn the city, but lack of wind allowed the pirate fleet to catch up with them, forcing the Spaniards to abandon the boats and continue on foot. As a result, the message could not be delivered in time.

On November 30, Limahong anchored at Isla del Corregidor and deployed Shogo on a night raid with 400 to 600 pirates to take the unsuspecting city by surprise. However, bad luck hit the pirate fleet as well.

Limahong had ordered the execution of the Spanish prisoners after arriving at the beach, since the pirates could no longer rely on the prisoners' knowledge of the area, Shogo's expedition ran into dangerous currents, lost three boats, and drifted by mistake toward Parañaque instead of Manila.
Attack on Goiti's house

The pirates were spotted after attacking several locals, who mistakenly believed that Shogo and his group were Muslim bandits from Borneo. Governor Martín de Goiti was informed at his house, near the old San Agustin Church, but dismissed the report. He sent only ten guards to find out what was happening, without informing the garrison.

The pirates quickly killed the guards and besieged the house, where Goiti's wife, Lucía del Corral, taunted them from the window. Infuriated by the insults, which were translated for him by the Portuguese, Shogo ordered the house to be set on fire after confirming that it was well fortified.

Finally understanding the dire situation, Goiti and the few men inside sallied out against the pirates in a desperate attack. The governor was elderly and convalescing from an illness at the time, but he jumped from a low window in his rush to engage the enemy.

They were all killed, and the pirates cut off their noses and ears as human war trophies, since Limahong had put up a bounty for every dead Spaniard. Del Corral was stripped and left for dead with a wound in the throat, while another woman in the house died before she could surrender herself.
The house was destroyed, the only survivors being Del Corral and the soldier and pilot Francisco de Astigarribia.
Attack on Manila

With Goiti dead, Shogo resumed his march towards Manila, dividing his force into three columns. However, although the governor's house was located some distance away, Lavezaris was warned by the blaze and gunshots, allowing him to raise the alarm in time for Manila to prepare.

Shogo's force was met outside the walls by a nearby team of twenty arquebusiers commanded by Lorenzo Chacón, who harassed them into halting. However, their numerical advantage allowed the pirates to encircle Chacón and press their attack, killing eight before the rest could cut their way toward the city.

The Chinese pirates pursued them, but another company of 20 Spanish soldiers under Alonso Velázquez attacked from the flank. Shogo, likely fearing the intervention of more Spanish reinforcements, called for a retreat to Cavite, where they had agreed to reunite with Limahong after the victory.
